text: This project studies five matched model pairs drawn from four compact open-weight model families: Qwen3, the Llama 3 family, Phi-4-mini, and Mistral-7B [1]–[4].

Instruction-tuned models at this scale are increasingly practical to run locally, because they fit on consumer GPUs and because low-bit compression has been developed explicitly for on-device and mobile inference [5]–[7].

Quantization evaluations commonly report perplexity or benchmark accuracy [8], [9], but those measures alone do not reveal whether an apparent reduction in harmful compliance is a genuine alignment change or a loss of capability.
Prior work also shows that behavioural and trustworthiness effects can depend on both the model and the quantization method [8]–[10].
HarmBench and XSTest provide complementary ways to measure these behaviours [11], [12].
TrustLLM evaluates trustworthiness across safety, truthfulness, fairness, robustness, privacy, and machine ethics [13].
DecodingTrust provides another broad assessment, with detailed testing of toxicity, stereotypes, privacy, robustness, and related properties [14].
SafetyBench focuses more directly on safety knowledge through a large bilingual multiple-choice benchmark [15].
The InstructGPT study shows how human feedback can make a much smaller aligned model preferable to a far larger base model [16].
HarmBench then supplies a standardised framework for automated red teaming and harmful-compliance evaluation [12].
Universal suffix attacks can transfer across prompts and models [17], and model-generated red-team prompts can uncover failure cases at scale [18].
MMLU measures broad academic and professional knowledge [19], while ARC-Challenge tests difficult science questions [20].
SafetyBench's multiple-choice format is valuable for safety knowledge, but knowing the correct policy answer is not the same as refusing a harmful request during generation [15].
Scaling work shows that larger models often tolerate reduced precision better than smaller ones, but the relationship depends on model scale and task [21].

SmoothQuant migrates activation difficulty into weights to enable W8A8 inference [22], while SparseGPT demonstrates that a different compression operation, pruning, can remove many weights in one shot [23].
NF4 was introduced with QLoRA as a four-bit data type suited to approximately normally distributed model weights [24].
LLM.int8 uses a different mixed-precision strategy that routes outlier features through a higher-precision path [25].
Modern neural networks are often poorly calibrated [26], and quantization-specific work reports that confidence changes concentrate on difficult or low-confidence inputs [27].
GPTQ uses approximate second-order information to minimise reconstruction error during weight quantization [6].

AWQ's motivating analysis identifies approximately 0.1%–1% of weights as salient; its implemented method protects their contribution through activation-aware scaling rather than a literal mixed-precision layout [5].
SmoothQuant addresses activation outliers through an equivalent transformation [22].
NF4 uses a codebook designed for the distribution of neural weights [24], while LLM.int8 separates outlier features into a higher-precision path [25].
Some methods require representative samples and an optimisation pass [5], [6], [22], while BitsAndBytes load-time quantization can be applied without a task-specific calibration set [24], [25].
Four-bit results are often close to full precision on aggregate tasks, especially as model size grows [7]–[9].

Marchisio et al. show that multilingual quantization effects differ by language, and on the paper's Japanese evaluation the human-assessed loss is substantially larger than the automatic-metric loss [28].
HarmLevelBench reports non-uniform safety changes across quantization methods and attack types [29].
Q-resafe similarly treats quantized safety degradation as a distinct problem and proposes quantization-aware repair [30].

In contrast, Decoding Compressed Trust finds that four-bit quantization broadly preserves the trustworthiness dimensions it studies, while more extreme compression and pruning produce larger damage [31].
OmniQuant learns weight-clipping and equivalent transformations during calibration [32].
Q-Misalign goes further by preparing a model whose misalignment is triggered by quantization [33].
Safety Layers argues that aligned behaviour can be concentrated in a subset of model layers [34].
Together with work on refusal directions [35] and shallow alignment [36], this provides a plausible mechanism by which quantization may affect safety decisions differently across prompts and models.
Some studies use refusal or toxicity as a safety proxy, others use broad trustworthiness suites, and HarmLevelBench grades the level of harm in a response [29].
Q-Misalign shows that an attacker can create a durable quantization-conditioned failure [33], and Exploiting LLM Quantization shows another security-relevant pathway [37].
Decoding Compressed Trust is the prior study most similar to this experiment because it observes broad four-bit preservation [31].
StrongREJECT was motivated by “empty jailbreaks”: cases in which a target does not refuse but also does not provide useful harmful information [38].
SORRY-Bench evaluates safety refusal across 44 fine-grained unsafe topics, 440 balanced instructions, 20 linguistic augmentations, and 7,040 human annotations used in its evaluator study [39].
JailbreakBench standardises attack resources, chat templates, system prompts, scoring, and attack-efficiency measures [40].
WildGuard spans direct and adversarial interactions and predicts prompt harmfulness, response harmfulness, and refusal [41].
JailbreakBench records these elements because otherwise two attack-success rates may not be comparable [40].
XSTest is small enough for detailed human inspection and deliberately targets lexical and pragmatic triggers [11].
OR-Bench contains 80,000 prompts across ten rejection categories, a hard subset of about 1,000 prompts, and 600 toxic controls; the final ICML study evaluates 32 models across eight families [42].
StrongREJECT introduces response quality into jailbreak evaluation [38].

SORRY-Bench grounds refusal evaluation in a human-in-the-loop taxonomy of unsafe topics, and scores refusal on an explicitly binary scale, leaving finer-grained harmfulness scoring as future work [39].

Finer-grained annotation schemes show that binary refusal labels are a simplification: Do-Not-Answer uses six action categories [43], and XSTest labels responses as full compliance, partial refusal, or full refusal [11].
Do-Not-Answer evaluates 939 risky prompts and 5,634 responses and finds that a trained 600-million-parameter classifier can be competitive with a much larger judge in aggregate [43].
Prometheus 2 provides an open evaluator for direct assessment and pairwise ranking under user-specified criteria [44].

MT-Bench reports more than 80% agreement between strong LLM judges and human preferences in its tested setting, while also documenting position bias, verbosity bias, self-enhancement, and limited grading ability on some reasoning questions [45].
Prometheus 2 is designed for evaluation under user-specified criteria [44], while WildGuard targets prompt harmfulness, response harmfulness, and refusal [41].

Prior studies on adversarial attacks demonstrate that targeted worst-case failures can occur [33], [37], while jailbreak research shows that robustness requires dedicated adversarial evaluation [40].
Studies on automated evaluators further underscore the necessity of validating model-based judges against human annotations [43], [44].
Work on how safety training fails under adversarial pressure provides a final caution [46].
Kharinaev et al. declare 31 paired comparisons and apply a multiplicity correction [10], whereas the other two evaluations emphasise aggregate retention across many tasks [8], [9].
The literature on automatic judging makes clear that measurement systems evolve [43], [44].
Prompt-level pairing is preserved in both the bootstrap interval [47] and the exact McNemar comparison [48].
Mistral-7B provides the largest model in scope [4].
For each pair and outcome, the effect is the quantized rate or accuracy minus the baseline value, and paired bootstrap confidence intervals preserve prompt-level pairing [47].
Binary outcomes are also tested with the exact McNemar test [48], which uses only discordant prompt pairs and whose null hypothesis is equal marginal probability within the pair.
Benjamini and Hochberg's false-discovery-rate procedure controls multiplicity across that family [49], and a result is described as surviving correction only when its adjusted q-value is below 0.05.
Cohen's kappa measures chance-corrected agreement between scorers [50].
Sample-size and minimum-detectable-effect calculations follow paired-proportion power analysis [51], [52].

The agreement analysis recognises that coefficient choice and prevalence affect interpretation [53], so the report presents the coefficient with raw agreement and task context instead of assuming that the conventional verbal bands of Landis and Koch [54] apply equally to every setting.
Llama Guard provides an open-weight comparison for safety classification used in the scorer sensitivity analysis [55], and its construct is deliberately broader than the HarmBench behaviour label.
Equivalence is assessed only where the pre-specified margin and test are appropriate, and the two one-sided tests procedure supplies the formal basis [56].
Data-contamination risk is disclosed because benchmark familiarity can inflate capability estimates [57].
LLM-as-a-judge research reports useful agreement with human preferences [45], while surveys catalogue position, verbosity, and other biases [58].
Comparison with human annotations is necessary because automatic labels are not free evidence [59].
Non-parametric sensitivity comparisons use the Wilcoxon procedure where applicable [60], and power interpretation follows standard behavioural-science guidance [61].
The result is closest to Decoding Compressed Trust, which reports broad preservation of trustworthiness at four bits and larger damage under more aggressive compression [31].
Kharinaev et al. report that quantization can degrade safety, and that no single method universally outperforms the others across models and bit-widths [10].
HarmLevelBench finds attack-dependent changes [29], while Q-resafe and Q-Misalign show that quantized safety can be both repaired and attacked [30], [33].
Reference [29] is a non-archival workshop paper distributed as a preprint.

Its smallest model is 7B, so the 1.7B regime where this study finds its capability effect is unsampled. Its safety dimensions are Perspective-API toxicity and trust perspectives, which yield no compliance rate.

The spread across methods at one bit-width exceeds any single effect, and NF4 is not among them. An “error” label folds incoherent output into the safety score, mixing capability loss into it.

HarmLevelBench [29] | Vicuna-13B-v1.5; AWQ, bit-width not reported | Human-annotated ASR on direct queries rises 33.9 to 44.6, a gain of 10.7 points | Human annotation; the same rows give +16.1 by string match and +1.7 by GPT judge | A 56-item severity-stratified set of the authors' own, so 10.7 points is six queries. Bit-width, decoding settings and baseline precision are all unreported, and the direction depends on which of the paper's three scorers is read.

Q-resafe [30] | Llama-2-7B-Chat; AWQ 4-bit vs the same fp16 checkpoint | ASR rises 29.8 to 37.1 points at τ=0.95; the gap runs 4.5 to 17.3 points across six sampling settings | Decoding-attack ASR: GPT-4 selects the highest-scoring response from 49 decoding configurations | Measured under an active decoding attack with GPT-4 best-of-49 selection. The same fp16 checkpoint scores 0.3 un-attacked, so almost all of the 29.8-point reference level is attack effect rather than direct-request behaviour.

Q-Misalign [33] | InternLM2-Chat-1.8B, Gemma-1.1-2B-it and Llama-2-7B-Chat; int8, the paper's default | Jailbreak success identical to the two decimals printed: 0.07 to 0.07, 0.05 to 0.05, 0.00 to 0.00 (proportions) | Not reported | The paper's control condition, at 8-bit with no 4-bit counterpart, on AdvBench rather than HarmBench. Its main conclusion jump to 0.97 belongs to a checkpoint the authors prepared to misbehave once quantized, and is not an effect of ordinary quantization.

In the IEEE version of record, Table 14 reports safety ratios and defines the difference as FP16 minus quantized, so a positive difference means that the quantized model was judged less safe, the opposite orientation to the attack success rates in the neighbouring rows [10].
And the only prior row measuring an unmodified checkpoint under ordinary quantization without an attack is Q-Misalign's control condition, which shows no change on three checkpoints [33].

Published safety findings span different settings: Kharinaev et al. and HarmLevelBench evaluate ordinary quantization [10], [29], Q-resafe uses an active decoding attack [30], and Q-Misalign studies a deliberately prepared checkpoint [33].
The scorer findings align with StrongREJECT's warning about empty jailbreaks [38] and SORRY-Bench's insistence that safety refusal be interpreted with utility [39].

The three large evaluations reviewed here report good average retention at four bits [7]–[9], but the Qwen3-1.7B MMLU loss shows that compact models and task subsets can still contain material failures.
Marchisio et al.'s multilingual result is methodologically relevant even though the present experiment is English-only [28].
JailbreakBench evaluates a model under an attack procedure [40], while Q-Misalign constructs a quantization-conditioned attack [33].
Qwen and other multilingual families may respond differently in non-Latin scripts, and prior work reports disparate quantization effects by language [28].
